title: A rules of thumb-based design sequence for diffuse daylight
research_question: To critically review, validate, reformulate, and combine previously proposed daylighting rules of thumb into a four-step design sequence for diffuse daylight in sidelit spaces, and to compare its merits to the LEED-NC 2.2 glazing factor method.

participants.description: 2304 simulated rectangular, sidelit rooms with varying dimensions, window properties, and external obstruction scenarios. All spaces had a window-head-height of 2.74m (9 ft).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 2304 unique 3D Radiance models of sidelit rooms. Variables included glazing transmittance (35%, 75%), ceiling reflectance (50%, 80%), window width (full façade, 50% centered), balustrade (glazed, opaque), window header (yes, no), space width (1.0, 1.8, 3.6 * window-head-height), sky angle (90°, 75°, 60°, 45°, 30°, 15°), and neighboring construction (continuous, discontinuous; same height as target, two-story target).

Enhanced LEED Glazing Factor (with obstruction correction)

findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: The Lynes formula approximates the average daylight factor based on light flux entering and absorbed by interior surfaces.
findings.quote: Upon first inspection the two prediction methods agree pretty well with an R² of 0.90 and a slope of 0.81.

findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: The Lynes formula tends to underestimate the mean daylight factor compared to Radiance simulations.
findings.quote: The mean bias error (MBE) and root mean square error (RMSE) for all spaces are –4% and 50%, respectively.

findings.antecedent: Lynes average daylight factor formula (Equation 2) prediction of DF > 2%
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor prediction of DF > 2%
findings.mechanism: Disagreement between methods on meeting a 2% DF target.
findings.quote: Lynes formula and Radiance disagree in 304 of all 2304 spaces (13%)

findings.antecedent: Lynes average daylight factor formula (Equation 2) prediction of DF > 2%
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor prediction of DF > 2%
findings.mechanism: The Lynes formula tends to be more conservative, predicting a lower DF than Radiance.
findings.quote: only 18 spaces (less than 1%) for which Lynes predicts a daylight factor above 2% while Radiance does not.

findings.antecedent: Modified Lynes average daylight factor formula (Equation 3)
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: The modified Lynes formula also approximates the average daylight factor well.
findings.quote: The correlation between the two data series is equally good as for the Lynes formula with an R² value of 0.90.

findings.antecedent: Modified Lynes average daylight factor formula (Equation 3)
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: The modified Lynes formula tends to yield slightly higher values than Radiance.
findings.quote: the slope of the best fit curve in Figure 5 is 1.13, i.e. the rule tends to yield slightly higher values than Radiance.

findings.antecedent: Modified Lynes average daylight factor formula (Equation 3) prediction of DF > 2%
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor prediction of DF > 2%
findings.mechanism: Disagreement between methods on meeting a 2% DF target.
findings.quote: Lynes modified and Radiance diverge in 208 spaces

findings.antecedent: Modified Lynes average daylight factor formula (Equation 3) prediction of DF > 2%
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor prediction of DF > 2%
findings.mechanism: The modified Lynes formula tends to be more optimistic, predicting a higher DF than Radiance.
findings.quote: the rule of thumb predicting for 158 spaces that the space meets the 2% requirement when Radiance predicts the opposite.

findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: The DFF is a direct measure of the relative amount of daylight flux entering a space, correlating with the mean daylight factor.
findings.quote: A strong correlation between the two quantities is visible with an R² of 0.87.

findings.consequent: Daylight feasibility factor (DFF)
findings.mechanism: A specific DFF value corresponds to a target mean DF.
findings.quote: a mean daylight factor distribution of 2% roughly corresponds to a daylight feasibility factor of 0.18.

findings.consequent: Daylight feasibility factor (DFF)
findings.mechanism: A specific DFF value corresponds to a target mean DF.
findings.quote: a daylight factor criterion of 3% would translate into a daylight feasibility factor of 0.088*3.0%~0.26.

findings.consequent: Ratio of mean daylight factor in front half to back half of space
findings.mechanism: Without obstructions, daylight penetration is more uniform, leading to a lower front-to-back ratio.
findings.quote: In the absence of external obstructions (sky angle of 90°) the ratio lies between 4.8 and 6.0.

findings.consequent: Ratio of mean daylight factor in front half to back half of space
findings.mechanism: Obstructions reduce daylight penetration, increasing the illuminance gradient and thus the front-to-back ratio.
findings.quote: With obstructions the ratio goes as high as 20.

findings.consequent: Allowable room depth for 3:1 front-to-back DF ratio
findings.mechanism: Without obstructions, daylight penetrates deeper, but the 3:1 ratio is met at shallower depths due to higher overall DF.
findings.quote: the allowable room depth lies between 0.9 and 1.3 times the window-head-height.

findings.consequent: Allowable room depth for 3:1 front-to-back DF ratio
findings.mechanism: With heavy obstructions, overall DF is lower, allowing for deeper rooms to still meet the 3:1 ratio.
findings.quote: The depth only rises to 2.5 times the window-head-height for a few very heavily obstructed spaces.

findings.consequent: No sky line depth rule
findings.mechanism: As obstructions increase (smaller sky angle), the 'no sky line' depth becomes a more conservative estimate of daylit area.
findings.quote: The no sky line limiting depth lies above those of the two other rules for sky angles above 45°.

findings.consequent: Lynes limiting depth, no sky line depth, and 2.5*h_window-head-height rule
findings.mechanism: At moderate obstruction levels, the different rules of thumb for limiting depth converge.
findings.quote: At around 45° all three methods more or less agree.

findings.antecedent: LEED-NC 2.2 glazing factor formula (Equation 16) without obstruction correction
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: The LEED formula does not account for external obstructions, leading to poor predictions in obstructed scenarios.
findings.quote: the glazing factor method fails in the presence of external obstructions (crosses).

findings.antecedent: LEED-NC 2.2 glazing factor formula (Equation 16) without obstruction correction, in spaces without external obstructions
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: Without obstructions, the LEED formula provides a reasonable approximation of the mean daylight factor.
findings.quote: While the two prediction methods agree reasonably well for spaces without external obstructions (black dots; R²=0.9; slope=0.8)

findings.antecedent: Enhanced LEED glazing factor method (Equation 17) with obstruction correction factor (0/90°)
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor
findings.mechanism: Adding an obstruction correction factor significantly improves the accuracy of the LEED glazing factor method across all obstruction scenarios.
findings.quote: the least square fit for all 2304 spaces now corresponds to R²=0.90 with a slope of 0.79

findings.antecedent: Enhanced LEED glazing factor method (Equation 17) prediction of DF > 2%
findings.consequent: Radiance-calculated mean daylight factor prediction of DF > 2%
findings.mechanism: Disagreement between methods on meeting a 2% DF target.
findings.quote: diverging results in 329 spaces and only 16 spaces in which the glazing factor prediction is over 2% when Radiance is not.

findings.consequent: Percentage of floor area with DF > 2%
findings.mechanism: Higher mean DF generally correlates with a larger percentage of the floor area meeting a minimum DF threshold.
findings.quote: the correlation between the two quantities is reasonably high.

findings.consequent: Percentage of floor area with DF > 2% reaching 75%
findings.mechanism: Even with a mean DF above 2%, achieving the LEED requirement of 75% of floor area with DF > 2% is not guaranteed, indicating a potential disconnect between mean DF and spatial uniformity.
findings.quote: the percentage of floor area with a daylight factor over 2% never reaches 75% for all 2304 spaces even though a large proportion of these spaces have a mean daylight factor over 2%.

findings.antecedent: Daylight feasibility formula (Equation 1 in reply to comments)
findings.consequent: Student confusion
findings.mechanism: The empirical constant 0.088 in the original formula was confusing to students, leading to a simplified version.
findings.quote: many students were confused as to where the 0.088 comes from

mechanisms: The adjusted effective aperture directly measures the relative amount of daylight flux entering a space, linking to its daylighting potential.
The Lynes formula approximates average daylight factor by equating incoming light flux to absorbed flux on interior surfaces.
External obstructions reduce incoming daylight, increasing the illuminance gradient and affecting the uniformity of daylight penetration.
The 'no sky line' depth and window-head-height rules provide simplified estimates of the daylit zone depth based on geometry and obstruction.
implementation_implications: The proposed four-step design sequence provides a reliable method for designing sidelit spaces to meet average daylight factor requirements, particularly useful in early design stages.
The sequence can help designers quickly identify potential daylit zones, choose appropriate dimensions, and determine glazing area/type.
The original Lynes formula (Equation 2) is recommended over the modified version (Equation 3) due to its more conservative predictions, offering a 'safety margin'.
The LEED-NC 2.2 glazing factor method is unreliable in the presence of external obstructions and should be enhanced with an obstruction correction factor (0/90°).
The LEED requirement of 75% of floor area with DF > 2% is difficult to achieve even with a mean DF > 2%, suggesting a potential disconnect between mean DF and spatial uniformity.
The design sequence should be complemented by solar gains and glare analysis, especially in sunny climates or unobstructed facades.
The sequence is best suited for standard sidelit spaces with mostly Lambertian surfaces and does not account for advanced daylighting techniques or internal partitions/furniture.
The daylight feasibility formula can be simplified to WWR > DF / (10 * Tvis * 0 / 90) to reduce student confusion.
The decision of what constitutes a 'well daylit' space and the interpretation of limiting depth rules ultimately rests with the designer.

limitations: The design sequence only considers diffuse daylight and ignores the effect of direct sunlight for glare and energy considerations.
The sequence is validated for 'empty' spaces; results may not be reliable if internal partitions or furniture (especially objects higher than 1.1m or near windows) are introduced.
The method cannot distinguish between specular vs. matte reflectances or highly reflective ceilings vs. walls/floors.
The effect of light-redirecting façade elements cannot be predicted.
The sequence has only been validated for sidelit spaces and clear glazings, requiring expansion to toplit spaces and a wider variety of façade elements.
Interior room reflectances are typically unknown at early design stages, making precise application challenging.
The design sequence does not take overall energy use and/or glare into account.
The daylight factor metric itself has known limitations, such as not taking local climate, façade orientation, or movable shading devices into account.

paper_metadata.title: A rules of thumb-based design sequence for diffuse daylight
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A rules of thumb-based design sequence for diffuse daylight
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper proposes and validates a daylighting design sequence for sidelit spaces. Since the design sequence uses the daylight factor as a performance metric, it is aimed towards spaces that primarily receive diffuse daylight. It should be complemented by a design analysis that looks at direct sunlight for glare and energy considerations. The sequence interconnects and refines earlier proposed rules of thumb and is intended to be used during the earliest design stages when concepts regarding programming, floor plans, massing and window areas are initially explored. All steps within the sequence were ‘validated’ using Radiance simulations of over 2300 sidelit spaces. During step one of the sequence the effective sky angles are calculated and target daylight factors are defined for all potential daylit zones within a building. In step two a refined version of the ‘daylight feasibility study’ is used to help the design team to identify building zones with high daylighting potential based on a target mean daylight factor criterion. During step three suitable interior room dimensions and surface reflectances are determined using a combination of the Lynes’ limiting depth, ‘no sky line’, and window-head-height rules of thumb. Step four provides a more accurate estimate of the required glazing area for each zone based on the Lynes daylight factor formula which is also validated as part of this work. The effect of external obstructions is considered throughout the process. The paper closes with a discussion of the merits of the design sequence compared to the glazing factor spreadsheet calculation method promoted by LEED-NC 2.2.
